posts.title: AI protiv AI: može li tehnologija koja generiše prevaru istovremeno da bude deo odbrane?
posts.author: Nikola Čučilović
posts.snippet:
AI protiv AI: može li tehnologija koja generiše prevaru istovremeno da bude deo odbrane?

Sa velikim zadovoljstvom delim da je objavljen naučni rad „Using AI to Combat AI-generated Fraud: A Semantic Detector with Blockchain Integration“, koji sam pripremio sa uvaženom koleginicom Tamarom Jušković. Rad je objavljen u časopisu *Journal of Computer and Forensic Sciences*.

Nismo želeli da ostanemo samo na opisu problema. Želeli smo da pokažemo kako bi tehnologija koja se zloupotrebljava za stvaranje prevara mogla istovremeno postati deo odbrane od njih.

U radu predstavljamo praktični prototip semantičkog detektora koji primenom NLP-a analizira značenje poruke, prepoznaje obrasce karakteristične za prevare i rezultate evidentira na blockchain mreži, radi očuvanja integriteta, transparentnosti i proverljivosti zapisa.

Iako se blockchain na prvi pogled najčešće povezuje sa kriptovalutama, njegov potencijal je mnogo širi. 

Može se koristiti za:

– potvrđivanje autentičnosti digitalnih dokaza i očuvanje njihovog lanca čuvanja;
– evidentiranje ko je, kada i na koji način pristupao određenim podacima;
– proveru porekla dokumenata, fotografija, video-zapisa i sadržaja generisanog veštačkom inteligencijom;
– zaštitu digitalnog identiteta i verifikaciju sertifikata i kvalifikacija;
– transparentnu razmenu podataka između institucija bez mogućnosti neprimetnog naknadnog menjanja zapisa.

Suština je jednostavna:  tehnologija koja omogućava da prevare postanu brže, uverljivije i personalizovanije može se upotrebiti i za njihovo ranije otkrivanje, analizu i sprečavanje.

Ovim konceptualnim modelom pokazali smo da odgovor na savremene prevare ne mora ostati spor, dominantno ručan i zasnovan samo na prepoznavanju ranije poznatih obrazaca. AI može analizirati kontekst i značenje, dok blockchain može obezbediti pouzdan i proverljiv trag o rezultatima takve analize.

Uspešna borba protiv visokotehnološkog kriminala zato ne podrazumeva samo regulisanje veštačke inteligencije i ograničavanje njene zloupotrebe. Ona zahteva i njenu odgovornu primenu kao alata za prevenciju, rano upozoravanje, zaštitu digitalnih dokaza i podršku istragama.

#ArtificialIntelligence #Cybercrime #DigitalForensics #Blockchain #Cybersecurity #Research
posts.reason: Academic research on AI-generated fraud detection with blockchain integration is relevant to compliance and forensics buyers, though the post is more about AI than crypto investigation.

comments.text: Beleženje rezultata detekcije na blockchainu je koristan potez za lanac čuvanja dokaza, ali u praksi je najveći izazov to što tužioci i sudije još uvek retko razumeju razliku između hash zapisa i stvarnog dokaza sadržaja — bez jasne metodologije, i najbolji model ostaje teško upotrebljiv na sudu.

Da li ste testirali model na multijezičnim ili prevedenim prevarnim porukama? U našoj praksi upravo tu semantički detektori najčešće gube preciznost jer se obrasci prevare menjaju sa jezikom i kulturnim kontekstom.

Iz iskustva sa forenzičkim izveštajima koji moraju biti upotrebljivi pred sudom, upravo je taj deo o proverljivosti zapisa presudan — tužioci i advokati mnogo lakše prihvataju nalaz kad mogu nezavisno da provere svaki korak analize, a ne samo konačan zaključak.

posts.title: A timely reminder that even the most trusted security solutions can have unexpected vulnerabilities.
posts.author: Jane Anderson
posts.snippet:
A timely reminder that even the most trusted security solutions can have unexpected vulnerabilities.
🔐 Key takeaways from this excellent article on the recent Coldcard exploit: 
• ⚠️ Around 1,816 bitcoin (approximately £86 million) is reported to have been lost after weaknesses in seed generation enabled attackers to reconstruct private keys. 
• 💻 The exploit highlights how software vulnerabilities, rather than user error, can compromise even hardware wallets designed for secure self-custody. 
• 🤖 The incident also raises important questions about the growing role of AI in identifying software vulnerabilities, for both defenders and attackers. 
• 🚨 For affected users, acting quickly to secure remaining assets, preserve evidence and seek appropriate legal advice may be critical. 
• 📈 More broadly, the case is a reminder that effective cyber risk management requires more than technology alone. Governance, incident response, forensic investigation and asset recovery strategies all have an important role to play. 
An interesting read from my colleague Asim Arshad exploring what happened, the potential legal implications, and the practical steps victims should consider.
👉🏼 https://lnkd.in/e_HAZC5f 
#CryptoAssets #CyberSecurity #DigitalAssets #Blockchain #AssetRecovery #CryptoDisputes #RiskManagement #LegalInsights
posts.reason: Substantive post by a legal professional on Coldcard exploit, asset recovery and forensic investigation that invites thoughtful discussion with lawyers and compliance professionals.

comments.text: Bitna distinkcija koju članak pravi je da je ovo softverska ranjivost u generisanju entropije, ne kompromitovanje self-custody modela kao takvog — što znači da praćenje sredstava nakon krađe i dalje zavisi od standardnih choke-point analiza na centralizovanim berzama gde se sredstva na kraju likvidiraju.

Zanima me da li je u ovom slučaju bilo dovoljno vremena za brzu reakciju pre nego što su sredstva slojevito prebačena kroz mixere - kod ovakvih propusta u entropiji brzina detekcije često određuje da li je uopšte moguće pratiti tok dalje.

U našim slučajevima gde je kompromitovan seed umesto samog uređaja, korisnici skoro uvek prekasno shvate obim problema jer prate samo jedan novčanik, dok napadač već testira više izvedenih adresa - upravo ta faza pre isplate je gde se najviše dokaza gubi.

Blockchain’s Next Challenge Is Rebuilding Trust After Security Failures

Blockchain technology continues to attract new users and institutional capital, but security incidents are leaving long-lasting damage across the industry.

Research from Immunefi found that approximately 84% of hacked tokens remained below their pre-attack prices six months after an incident. The affected assets recorded a median decline of 61%, showing that the the financial impact of an exploit often continues long after the stolen funds have been transferred.

Immunefi examined 425 publicly disclosed incidents between 2021 and 2025, representing combined losses of approximately $11.9 billion. Major attacks can reduce the value of project treasuries, weaken liquidity, delay product development and limit the resources available to compensate users. The findings highlight why audits alone are not enough. Blockchain projects also need continuous monitoring, diversified treasuries, incident-response plans and clear recovery procedures.

The Coldcard hardware-wallet vulnerability has added another layer to the trust debate. The incident reportedly exposed weaknesses in private-key generation and contributed to losses exceeding $100 million. Following the case, OKX reported increased inflows as some users moved assets away from self-custody and back towards centralised platforms.

At the same time, romance scams and other forms of social engineering continue to target crypto users across Asia. These attacks show that secure code cannot protect individuals from emotional manipulation or fraudulent investment platforms.

Blockchain trust therefore depends on the entire ecosystem, including smart contracts, hardware, custodians, governance structures and user education. The projects most likely to succeed will be those that make these dependencies visible and prepare realistic recovery mechanisms before a crisis occurs.

Why would the world's largest spot ether ETF cut its trading costs from 7 basis points to roughly 2 — right as ether sits nearly 40% down year-to-date?

BlackRock (https://lnkd.in/dAjA5nP) has filed an 8-K with the SEC (https://lnkd.in/e36jGfab) for a 1-for-3 reverse split of ETHA, its iShares Ethereum Trust ETF, effective October 6, 2026. The share price is expected to move from roughly 14 to roughly 42 dollars, with zero impact on the fund's total value. The record date is October 5, and the consolidation will be fully automatic through brokerage platforms — no action required from shareholders.

The real story is cost structure, not price. Bloomberg's Eric Balchunas notes the split should bring ETHA's trading costs down to about 2bps from 7bps, compared to fees of up to 140bps on crypto-native exchanges. With over 5 billion dollars in AUM, ETHA remains the largest spot ether ETF, ahead of Grayscale's competing fund.

There is a real operational risk investors should note: residual fractional shares will be settled in cash, and that cash-out can trigger unexpected tax events for holders in taxable accounts. This is a mechanical consequence of the split, not a market call, but it deserves attention before the October record date.

This filing signals that the ETF wrapper is no longer just competing with crypto-native exchanges on access to ether — it is now competing on execution cost, and BlackRock has just reset the benchmark for what institutional-grade ether exposure should cost.

Whether the market reads this purely as plumbing or as a subtler signal about the maturity of regulated crypto infrastructure will shape how other issuers respond in the coming quarters.

Crypto has moved from niche experiment to global financial infrastructure — touching payments, investment markets, FX, banking, and cross-border commerce. The question regulators are asking today isn't "should crypto exist?" It's "how should it operate within the financial system?"

Here's what's actually driving the rules:

𝟭. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿 & 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — FTX and Terra/Luna wiped out billions and exposed weak custody and governance practices.

𝟮. 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲 — AML/KYC in the US, MiCA licensing in the EU.

𝟯. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 — stablecoins like USDT and USDC now move billions daily; regulators want to know what backs them.

𝟰. 𝗟𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘆 — Dubai's VARA and the EU's MiCA give businesses clear rules before they commit capital.

𝟱. 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — Singapore and Hong Kong are proving regulation can attract institutional capital, not just restrict it.

𝟲. 𝗧𝗮𝘅𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 — trading profits, staking rewards, and token sales are now taxable income in the US, UK, and Nigeria.

𝟳. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 — Nigeria's shift from restricting crypto banking in 2021 to formal regulatory recognition shows the global pattern: restriction gives way to supervised adoption.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗳𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲: Adoption here isn't speculative — it's driven by currency instability, cross-border payment needs, and demand for dollar liquidity. Nigeria and South Africa are showing the continent's move toward supervised, not restricted, digital asset markets.

The bottom line: The future belongs to jurisdictions that balance consumer protection, financial stability, and innovation — not to those that ignore regulation or over-restrict it. Good policy doesn't remove opportunity. It builds the foundation for a sustainable digital asset economy.

— OG ATTAH | DYNAMIQ ALPHA

The gambling industry is entering a new era of regulatory complexity — driven by cryptocurrencies, prediction markets and increasingly sophisticated financial crime.

In the foreword to the International Gambling Laws & Regulations Review 2026/27, John Stawyskyj, Consultant at Ashurst Perkins Coie and Board Member of the International Association of Gaming Advisors (IAGA), explores the global regulatory trends reshaping the gambling sector and the challenges regulators will face in the years ahead.

As gambling markets continue to evolve, jurisdictions across the world are being challenged to balance innovation, market growth and consumer protection within an increasingly interconnected regulatory environment.

Key themes explored in the foreword include:

◆ The rapid growth of cryptocurrency gambling and the regulatory challenges surrounding transparency, consumer protection and anti-money laundering
◆ The emergence of prediction markets and their increasingly blurred distinction between financial products and gambling services
◆ The importance of international cooperation in combating illegal gambling, offshore operators and financial crime
◆ Expanding regulatory frameworks across Latin America, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region
◆ The growing need for cross-border intelligence sharing and coordinated enforcement
◆ The impact of regulatory fragmentation on operators, compliance and global market growth
◆ The importance of balancing technological innovation with robust regulatory oversight

The foreword highlights that while technological innovation continues to create significant opportunities for the global gambling industry, fragmented regulation, black-market activity and evolving financial crime require regulators to work together more closely than ever before. As gambling, financial markets and blockchain technology increasingly converge, international cooperation will play a critical role in maintaining market integrity and protecting consumers.

🔍 Day Two of the Association of Certified Financial Crime Specialists - ACFCS's FinCrime Virtual Week 2026, themed “Myths and Legends,” reinforced a profound truth 👉🏽 that financial-crime threats never emerge in isolation; they evolve where technology, culture, regulation, and commerce converge

🔮 Building on this theme, Michael Hornsby and Michelle Kendler-Kretsch from the Anti-Corruption Data Collective presented “Illicit Oracles” to demonstrate how prediction markets can enable insider trading, corruption, and manipulation. Their detailed analysis on the subject had deepened my understanding of blockchain tracing and the importance of coordinated controls across banks, crypto exchanges, and market platforms

🪙 Extending that insight, Ross Delston, CAMS, CTCE, and Timothy Dunfey Esq.,’s “The (Stable)Coin of the Realm” illustrated why stablecoin innovation must be matched by safeguards against scams, sanctions evasion, money laundering, and third-party risk. Shifting from regulation to investigation, Paolo Walcher’s “The Path through the Labyrinth” explored how OSINT, Arabic naming conventions, multilingual searches, and cultural context can transform information into actionable intelligence

🧭 Translating risk into action, Maleka Ali and Steve Wallace, CAMS’s “Risk Assessments: From Red Flags to Rabbit Holes,” connected strategy with execution, exemplifying how risk scores create value when converted into defensible priorities, proportionate escalation, and well-supported investigative decisions

🚭 Bringing these lessons into a tangible local context, “Vape and Mirrors,” presented by Dr. Zoya Faynleyb, CRCM, CAMS, CAFP, and Bart McEntire, resonated amid the recent Singapore’s illegal-vaping surge, drug-laced products, and growing health concerns among youths. By connecting counterfeiting and trade-based money laundering with transnational criminal networks, the session showcased why compliance professionals must look beyond surface-level regulatory breaches to trace suspicious payment flows, import-export anomalies, illicit supply chains, and organised-crime exposure

👏 My sincere appreciation goes out again to Erin O'Loughlin, CAMS, CFCS, Brian Svoboda-Kindle, and Cheyenne Vyska for moderating with panache and grace, keeping the conversations dynamic, focused, and engaging for all participants

🌐 Collectively, these thought-provoking sessions have sharpened my ability to identify emerging typologies, assess risk within its wider context, and convert intelligence into practical, forward-looking controls, supporting my continued growth as an informed, adaptable, and effective risk and compliance professional

posts.title: **🔺 Financial crime is not a single event—it's an interconnected ecosystem.**
posts.author: The FinCrime Institute
posts.snippet:
**🔺 Financial crime is not a single event—it's an interconnected ecosystem.**

Behind every suspicious transaction lies a much larger network of activities, facilitators, and criminal objectives. To disrupt financial crime effectively, AML professionals must understand **how every layer connects to the next**.

The foundation often begins with **predicate crimes** such as fraud, cybercrime, corruption, human trafficking, tax evasion, or drug trafficking. These crimes generate illicit proceeds that criminals seek to disguise.

To move those funds, they rely on **enablers**—money mules, shell companies, front businesses, fake documentation, and professional facilitators—who help conceal ownership, obscure audit trails, and create an appearance of legitimacy.

Next come the **money laundering methods**. Whether through Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML), cash smuggling, structuring, crypto assets, or offshore transfers, the objective remains the same: separate illicit funds from their criminal origin.

Finally, criminals exploit the **financial system**—banks, fintechs, payment providers, MSBs, and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)—to move value across borders and integrate illicit proceeds into the legitimate economy.

This is why AML professionals must think beyond individual transactions. Effective investigations require understanding the **entire financial crime ecosystem**, identifying how different actors, methods, and entities interact, and recognizing where intervention can have the greatest impact.

Every layer of the pyramid presents an opportunity to disrupt criminal networks.

✔️ Strong Customer Due Diligence (CDD)
✔️ Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD)
✔️ Transaction Monitoring
✔️ Network & Link Analysis
✔️ Beneficial Ownership Identification
✔️ Information Sharing
✔️ Timely SAR/STR Reporting

These controls don't just detect suspicious activity—they help dismantle the infrastructure that enables financial crime.

💬 **Question for the AML community:**
**Which layer of the Financial Crime Pyramid do you believe presents the greatest challenge for investigators to detect and disrupt—and why?**

#AML #FinancialCrime #AntiMoneyLaundering #FinCrime #Compliance #RiskManagement #CDD #EDD #TransactionMonitoring #TBML #CryptoCompliance #FraudPrevention #FinancialIntelligence #TheFinCrimeInstitute #AMLTraining
posts.reason: Deep discussion of AML/FIU ecosystem and financial crime networks directly targets compliance and AML officers with genuine educational content that invites expert contribution.

comments.text: One point worth stressing on the crypto layer specifically: TBML and cash smuggling take weeks to unwind, but on-chain layering can move value through a dozen addresses and cross-chain bridges within hours. Transaction monitoring that isn't tuned to that speed differential will always be reacting to a trail that's already gone cold.

Where do you see the weakest link in practice - is it EDD at onboarding, or the fact that most VASPs still can't do real-time cross-chain link analysis once funds start moving through swaps and mixers?

In tracing work we consistently see the same pattern: the predicate crime is solved, the enablers are known, but the case stalls at the exchange choke-point because the freeze request arrives days after the funds have already been converted and withdrawn.

posts.title: The RBI held the repo rate at 5.25% today — unchanged for the fourth consecutive meeting. On the surface, a non-event. Underneath, it's worth tracing through to what it actually do
posts.author: Yash Shrimali
posts.snippet:
The RBI held the repo rate at 5.25% today — unchanged for the fourth consecutive meeting. On the surface, a non-event. Underneath, it's worth tracing through to what it actually does to this sector.

The Governor's language is the real signal here, not the rate itself. He flagged that "the risk of second-round effects from higher food, fuel and other input costs translating into broader-based inflation persists." Rates held flat, but inflation risk explicitly called out as unresolved. That's a "hold" markets read as cautious, not comfortable.

Here's how that moves through wealth management and AMCs, step by step.

A hold with a hawkish tone still shifts expectations for where rates go next. Government bond yields adjust first, since they price in future policy, not just today's decision.

Bond prices and yields move inversely — so as yields adjust, existing bond holdings reprice. Debt mutual funds feel this immediately, and longer-duration funds feel it hardest.

Equity valuations move next, through a more basic mechanism: a stock's value is the present value of its future cash flows, discounted back at a rate tied to the risk-free rate. Nudge that discount rate up, and the exact same future earnings are worth less today — no change to the business itself required.

Since most fee revenue in this sector is a percentage of assets under management, both of those valuation moves hit revenue directly, with no lag.

Client behaviour shifts alongside this. When deposit and bond yields look relatively more attractive against equity risk, some client money reallocates out of funds and into fixed income — a demand-side pressure stacking on top of the valuation-side one.

One channel moves the opposite way. Loan-against-securities rates and NBFC lending yields are often tied to the same policy rate, so a firm's lending book can partially offset what its AUM book loses — the one part of this chain that doesn't point in the same direction as the rest.

And underneath all of it sits the quieter effect: if inflation risk is rising faster than nominal rates are, real returns on "safe" instruments are shrinking even when nothing on the rate sheet has technically moved. That's today's actual scenario — a flat headline number, with the real story sitting in the inflation commentary next to it.

posts.title: Can we find patterns in conversations?
posts.author: Alexander Lawrence

Can we find patterns in conversations?

Recently I've been fortunate to have spoken with a variety of people with some useful viewpoints at the GSMA, Vodafone IoT, Amdocs, Quadron, E^NATIP, Tecnotree Corporation, NI (National Instruments) and others, with write-ups published or soon-to-be on TelcoForge. The conversations have ranged across satellite, trust, AI, intelligent vision, data orchestration and more. On one level, it's a jumble, and especially if you focus on the technology. 

However, there seems to be an underlying concern in all these conversations which, five years ago, you'd be hard-pressed to find. They might formulate it differently, but the question of "What is the technology doing to us or for us?" seems to be a preoccupation. Whether that's about finding the right governance to create good outcomes; taking new approaches to support human thriving; or exploring how to architect a tech stack that works optimally for customers, it seems as though perspectives have changed. 

In the 2010s the zeitgeist seemed to be that the market would shape cool technology into uses that benefitted humanity as well as businesses. Working on #MWC agendas we tried to include societal topics, but people thought of it mainly about "connecting the unconnected" - that done, fortune would follow. It was hard to find proper conversations outside of a specific niche. 

So why the change? I'd welcome your thoughts on this. My guess is that it may be a few reasons - let me know if any resonate and what I'm missing.
 
1) The last few years of GPT fever have showed us all the risks and downsides of technology applied without care - it's not for 'somebody out there' any more.
2) Many telecoms players are dreading heavy infrastructure investment cycles and looking for solutions or approaches that deliver more bang for buck - which may mean, for example, doing things differently with what you already have rather than replacing it. 
3) Disillusionment with an online experience which can be bluntly poisonous to our wellbeing, which the lockdowns in COVID emphasised. There are good reasons to want to limit kids' screen time, to protect ourselves from the scams and misinformation and slop. Maybe, just maybe, there's another way... and if so, maybe telcos have an opportunity to mediate that change or insert themselves in a way that repositions them in the value chain. 

Does any of that make sense in your experience, or am I overthinking things?

posts.title: Paying the ransom is not a recovery plan, though plenty of businesses treat it like one.
posts.author: Michael Lai
posts.snippet:
Paying the ransom is not a recovery plan, though plenty of businesses treat it like one.

When ransomware hits, the instinct is to see the payment as the fix. Send the crypto, get the key, move on. The data says it does not work that cleanly.
Sophos surveyed 3,400 organizations hit by ransomware last year. Among those that paid, the payment bought a decryption key, not a clean recovery. The average cost to recover, on top of any ransom, came to US$1.53 million. That is the forensics, the rebuild, the downtime, the legal work. The ransom is the small line on the invoice.

And paying does nothing about the leak. In 28% of encryption cases the attackers had already stolen the data before locking it. A decryption key unlocks your files. It does not pull your customer records back off the criminal's server or stop them from publishing.

This changes what a broker should stress at renewal. The extortion payment is the part clients fixate on and the smallest part of the loss. The real questions are whether the policy funds a fast, expert incident response, covers business interruption for the days offline, and handles the notification and liability when stolen data surfaces.

A client with strong backups and a tested response plan recovers without the attacker's key. A client who planned to pay their way out finds out how much the key does not cover.

Ready before it happens beats paying after.

posts.title: The Coldcard hack didn't happen once. It happened four times — and it might not be over.
posts.author: Nese Unsal
posts.snippet:
The Coldcard hack didn't happen once. It happened four times — and it might not be over.
Here's the timeline, because the "why now" only makes sense once you see it laid out:
→ July 30: An attacker drains 1,196 Bitcoin addresses in 41 minutes. ~$70M gone. 
→ August 1: A second wave hits. Running total: ~$75M, now 2,673 addresses. → August 2–3: A third wave. ~$89M, 4,585 addresses. 
→ August 4: Multiple different attacker groups are now confirmed active. Total: ~$130M.
Same root cause each time. Different attackers.

The bug itself: a March 2021 firmware change in Coldcard wallets quietly broke the link to the device's hardware random number generator. Instead of using true hardware entropy to create your seed phrase, some devices fell back to a software-based generator seeded from the chip's serial number and timer state — both of which are guessable. On older models, the effective randomness collapsed to roughly 40 bits. For context, a 12-word seed is supposed to carry 128 bits of entropy. That gap is the whole story.

Here's the part worth sitting with: no device was ever touched. No password was stolen. The cryptography worked exactly as designed. The flaw was upstream, at the moment the seed was created — years before any of these victims ever signed a transaction.

Why does it keep escalating instead of being a one-time event?
Because the vulnerable population isn't a single wallet — it's every seed generated by affected firmware since 2021 that hasn't been rotated. Coinkite shipped a firmware fix, but a firmware update doesn't repair a seed that was already weak. The only real fix is generating a brand-new seed on the patched firmware and migrating funds — and that requires the owner to act. Every wallet that hasn't moved yet is still sitting in the same guessable keyspace, which is exactly why several independent attacker groups are now scanning and racing each other to it.

Will there be more?
Realistically, yes — until the remaining exposed wallets are emptied or migrated, whichever comes first. This isn't a contained incident anymore; it's an open race between owners and attackers over the same finite set of addresses.

The broader point, beyond Coldcard specifically:
This is the same pattern behind most crypto losses this year, according to Blockaid's H1 2026 data — the majority of stolen value doesn't come from smart contract exploits. It comes from compromised keys and operational failure points that sit outside the transaction itself: weak seed generation, phishing, blind approvals.

Self-custody was supposed to remove counterparty risk. It didn't remove risk — it relocated it, to whatever generated or is about to sign your keys. "Not your keys, not your coins" is still true. But it's incomplete. 

The real question is: what generated those keys, and do you actually know what you're approving before you sign?

That's the layer most of the industry still isn't watching.

#Bitcoin #CryptoSecurity #Web3 #SelfCustody #SureStack

comments.text: The forty-versus-128-bit gap is the number that matters here — it's not a small degradation, it collapses the seed into a keyspace an attacker can brute-force with commodity hardware, which explains why multiple independent groups are racing the same wallets rather than one actor draining quietly.

Is there any visibility into how the swept funds are moving post-theft — straight to centralized exchanges, or through mixers and bridges first? That would say a lot about how much of the $130M is realistically recoverable versus already unreachable.

On the tracing side, the multi-wave pattern you describe is a giveaway of parallel, uncoordinated actors: coordinated single-group thefts tend to move funds in a tight window, while separate groups scanning the same keyspace produce exactly this kind of staggered, escalating timeline.

The cause was a setting configured wrong when a new strategy went live on July 13. 

But how come nobody caught it?

Protocols cap how much money can leave at once so an attacker cannot drain everything in one move, and this withdrawal was small enough to pass under every limit. 

The safety system was built for the catastrophic version of the event, so the smaller one walked straight through it.

Feels like these kind of attacks are shaping 2026. 

There have already been 212 verified exploits and more than $1.1 billion stolen in six months.

This is the most hacked half year in crypto's history by incident count. More than one breach per day. 

Most of those attacks are small bugs carrying small amounts, which is exactly the range that clears a system watching for a nine figure drain.

So what's the solution?

Tighter thresholds that catch the small stuff and annoy every legitimate user, or a treasury big enough to cover the losses that get through?

posts.title: 📋 Which token disclosure regime actually protects investors?
posts.author: Axis Group

📋 Which token disclosure regime actually protects investors?

As the crypto market matures, two frameworks have been adopted cementing what issuers must tell investors about their tokens. The EU's MiCA regulation mandates comprehensive whitepaper disclosure at issuance. Blockworks Token Transparency Framework (TTF) provides a voluntary, industry-led standard for ongoing post-launch transparency.

Which one better serves investor interests and what can each learn from the other?

We've analyzed both regimes side-by-side in a new post. Key findings:

✓ MiCA's approach is more rigorous: it requires substantive quality standards, named management attestation, and statutory civil liability. Enforcement is tied to market access and non-compliance can trigger withdrawal of admission to trading.

✓ The TTF captures what MiCA was never designed to track: post-launch disclosure (governance changes, buybacks, KOL marketing arrangements, security incidents). For tokens outside EU jurisdiction, it remains the primary transparency mechanism.

✓ There's convergence potential: the TTF could strengthen its credibility with institutional investors by adopting six specific elements from MiCA - a quality standard distinct from completeness, defined update triggers, machine-readable schema, and more.

This analysis is grounded in Axis Group's direct experience drafting and submitting MiCA whitepapers in Malta, and reflects current Blockworks framework documentation.

Read the full comparative analysis here: https://lnkd.in/eFpqT8di

Which framework best protects investors in your market?

#TokenTransparency #MiCA #CryptoRegulation #InvestorProtection #Crypto
posts.reason: MiCA and token disclosure regimes are directly relevant to our regulatory and compliance buyer segment, and this substantive comparative analysis invites meaningful discussion from firms like ours.

comments.text: One practical gap in both frameworks: neither mandates disclosure of post-issuance security incidents in a standardized, timely format, which is exactly the data an investor or a forensic reviewer needs when a token's smart contract or bridge is later exploited.

Does the TTF's voluntary status create a selection problem — are the issuers most likely to have something to hide also the ones least likely to adopt it, leaving investors with a transparency signal that's really just a self-selection signal?

Drafting MiCA whitepapers is one thing; verifying that the source-of-funds behind a token issuance matches what's disclosed is another — we consistently find the gap between what's attested and what's traceable on-chain is where the real investor risk sits, and neither framework fully addresses that.

posts.author: Michael Ross

The actual Squid Game crypto scam contract is still sitting on the blockchain. I read it.
November 2021: a token cashing in on the Netflix show went from $0.01 to $2,861 in days. Then the developers pulled $3.38 million out of the liquidity pool and the price hit zero in minutes. International news story.
The contract is still public. Verified source code, right there on BscScan. So I ran it through my free checker.
Two things stood out.
First: the owner could change the contract's logic at any time — swap it for anything, whenever they wanted.
Second, and this is the part that got me: the function controlling owner privileges isn't named "onlyOwner" like every normal contract. They named it "ifSir."
Not a typo. Not an accident. A disguised name, on a function that let them do whatever they wanted with your money, hiding in plain sight in verified, public code the entire time.
Nobody had to guess this token was risky. It was written directly into the contract, in a modifier they thought nobody would bother reading.
That's the whole point of reading the code instead of trusting the chart.
Free tool if you want to check one yourself: nexustrinity.io/check
What's the most obvious red flag you've ever seen hiding in plain sight?

posts.title: In this deepening search for integrity within regeneration itself, oftentimes I find myself in bouts of grief and disbelief.
posts.author: Gertie Farenas
posts.snippet:
In this deepening search for integrity within regeneration itself, oftentimes I find myself in bouts of grief and disbelief.

Alongside that is the growing curiosity around reconnecting with my Global South origins, especially as a Southeast Asian.

The fundamental discord between the relational cultures of the Global North and Global South remains evident in today’s discussions about what regeneration demands.

(No, I am not dropping that distinction, unless that distinction is fully acknowledged with humility. That core difference taints every single decision within that space and beyond, and I can’t stay blind from this anymore.)

More importantly, I am identifying the core of my grief coming from that discord—because intentionality can be murky when the root of the disconnection has never changed.

I find myself wanting to call this out multiple times even when it seems futile to do so.
Exclusive “communities” that dismiss the realities of the locals.

Adoption of concepts from our lands without proper credit (and worse, distortion of such concepts  to sanitize their image more than they can admit).

Complicated structures to add to the “regenerative space” while the ones working on the land aren’t given what they need (and often remain underfunded — to the point that it feels so contradicting whenever people from the Global North question our “lack of participation” in spaces that are logistically and financially more affordable for them than us). 

I say these things as someone who continuously navigates these tensions and coexisting ironies. I find them confronting, too.

We scream of regeneration when these lands have just been affected more recently while we’ve carried the brunt of climate change for years before theirs.

posts.author: Monipal
posts.snippet:
18.7% of people in Malta live in a household that could not settle an unexpected expense of around €950.

Source: National Statistics Office Malta, EU-SILC 2025.

It is easy to read that as a poverty figure and move on, but €950 is a washing machine, a car repair or a vet bill, and those are the ordinary interruptions of a normal life rather than exceptional costs. They arrive without asking whether the month was convenient.

Which means a meaningful share of these households are managing perfectly well month to month. Income covers outgoings. Nothing looks wrong from the outside, and often nothing feels wrong from the inside either. What is missing is the buffer... the famous Emergency Fund.

The buffer is invisible in a way income is not. Colleagues cannot see it, friends cannot see it, and quite often the household has never worked out where it stands until something breaks and the answer arrives all at once.

That gap is not about income, and it is not about willpower. It is about people not having a clear enough view of their own position to act on it early. 

Building that view, and making it something people actually engage with rather than avoid, is the problem Monipal exists to work on.

Finding free versions of software, movies, games, music, or premium tools online can be tempting. With just a few clicks, users can access content without paying a fee. However, what appears to be a harmless shortcut often comes with serious cybersecurity risks. 
Illegal download websites are among the most common channels cybercriminals use to distribute malware, steal sensitive information, and compromise devices. The real cost of these downloads is often far greater than the money saved.

These are few reasons why illegal download sites are dangerous: 
1.  Many illegal download sites are designed to collect user some information such as login credentials, banking information, personal documents, company data or more.
2. Attackers frequently hide malicious software inside files that appear safe, it could be downloaded movie, application, document or game which may contain malware that silently installs itself on your device and this act can slow down or damage your device, corrupt important files, monitor your online activities or have unauthorized access to your system.
3. Illegal websites often use deceptive advertisements and multiple download buttons to trick users into clicking malicious links and these links may redirect users to fake websites that mimic trusted brands and request sensitive information such as usernames, passwords or payment details.

These are few measures to stay safe: 
1. Download software only from official websites and trusted app stores.
2. Verify website URLs before downloading any file.
3. Keep antivirus and security software up to date.
4. Avoid clicking suspicious pop-ups or advertisements.
5. Regularly update your operating system and applications.
6. Report suspicious websites to your IT or cybersecurity team.

When something online appears too good to be true, it usually is. Illegal download websites may promise free access to content, but they often expose users to malware, data theft, ransomware and other cyber threats.
The safest download is one that comes from a trusted and authorized source.
